comments.text: My grandfather was a farrier. He ran away from home at 14 during the Great Depression and joined the Army. He volunteered for the Cavalry, and completed the Cavalry School at the age of 15. It was a tough course, men were assigned to horses, not the other way around, the Army paid more money for the horses than the men. My grandfather learned to be a farrier while in the Cavalry, as well as training new horses. He rose through the ranks becoming Stable Sergeant, at which point “they took the horses away." Then WW2 broke out, and he was sent to the Pacific. At the end of the war he was one of only 2 members of his troop to return home. He then worked as a farrier, working at Arlington and Fort Belvoir as a civilian. He was regarded as the best farrier in the business, and worked on president Eisenhower's horses, and then Kennedy's. He eventually moved to the Southwest, and a full page article in the local paper was written about his life, after which he never wanted for work. When I was a kid I often rode along with him as he worked. He was good at his job, but as good a farrier as he was, he was a better rider. Growing up around horses, and spending time at tracks, show rings, and rodeos, and being a rider myself, there were few people as masterful on horseback as my grandfather. When he died, he was buried at the national cemetery.
